questions.question: What is PreparedStatement in JDBC and why is it preferred?
questions.title: PreparedStatement in JDBC — Overview and Benefits
questions.direct_answer: PreparedStatement represents SQL with parameter placeholders and typed binding methods. It is the normal choice for values because parameters preserve SQL structure and prevent those values from becoming injected syntax. Repeated execution can reduce parsing or improve batching, but precompilation and plan reuse depend on the driver, database, connection, and configuration, so it is not universally faster.

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether you know PreparedStatement's two big wins: safety and reuse.
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Treating it as security-only, or still concatenating values.
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Mention it also handles type conversion and escaping correctly for you.

sections.title: PreparedStatement: Parameters First, Performance Conditional
sections.content:
PreparedStatement also provides type conversion, batch methods, and generated-key requests. It is not a tool for dynamic identifiers: ORDER BY ? binds a value, not a column name. Select dynamic columns or directions from an allow-list and concatenate only the trusted mapped token.

A prepared statement belongs to its Connection and should be closed. The database can still choose different plans for different parameter values or invalidate cached plans after schema/statistics changes.

sections.title: Quick revision
content: Bind values with ? and setXxx methods; placeholders cannot stand for table or column names.
Parameterization is the primary SQL-injection defense for data values.
Reuse one PreparedStatement on the same connection for repeated work or batches.
Treat plan caching and server preparation as implementation details to measure.

sections.title: Interview answer
sections.content: SELECT * FROM users WHERE email = ? fixes the query structure and binds the email separately at the JDBC API level. An input containing quotes or SQL operators remains one value. The driver may use a server-prepared statement, a client-side protocol, or an emulated path; the safety comes from parameter semantics, not from the claim that every database compiled the SQL once before seeing any values. Reuse and batching may improve performance, but validate with the target driver.

sections.title: PreparedStatement at a Glance
sections.content:
emerald|Safety|~injection-proof|? placeholders|values bound as data|SQL parsed first
blue|Performance|~precompiled|parse + plan once|rebind + run|fast in loops/batches
amber|Convenience|~handles formatting|type conversion|escaping quotes/dates|NULL handling
rose|vs Statement|~the default|Statement = static only|PreparedStatement = with input|always prefer

sections.title: PreparedStatement vs Statement
sections.content:
| Aspect | Statement | PreparedStatement |
|---|---|---|
| Parameters | none (concatenate) | `?` placeholders |
| SQL injection | vulnerable | safe |
| Precompiled | no | yes |
| Repeated execution | re-parsed each time | plan reused |
| Escaping/types | manual | automatic |

sections.title: Statement: concatenated, unsafe, re-parsed
sections.content:
```java
Statement st = con.createStatement();
String sql = "SELECT * FROM users WHERE email = '" + email + "'"; // injectable
ResultSet rs = st.executeQuery(sql);  // re-parsed every call
```

sections.title: PreparedStatement: parameterized, safe, reusable
When to Use It
sections.content: Use **`PreparedStatement`** for essentially every query that has parameters or runs more than once — which is almost all real queries. Reserve plain `Statement` for static, parameterless one-off SQL like DDL.

seo.metaTitle: PreparedStatement in JDBC — Overview and Benefits — java backend interview question | InterviewExplainer
seo.metaDescription: Interview answer for What is PreparedStatement in JDBC and why is it preferred? with a clear explanation, practical example, common mistakes, and follow-up questions.

speakable_v2.hook: PreparedStatement does two jobs at once. It blocks SQL injection, and it runs faster each time you repeat a query.
speakable_v2.standard_example: A Java app querying a MySQL orders table by customer id with JDBC

beats.text: A PreparedStatement is a SQL query with question-mark placeholders for its values. You write the query once, then fill each placeholder with a typed setter like setString or setInt. The database compiles it one time.
It fixes two pains of a plain Statement. Gluing values into the SQL text invites injection, and that text gets re-parsed on every call. Placeholders close both gaps at once.

items: Placeholders mark each value spot. The first question mark is parameter one, not zero.
Typed setters bind the values. You pick setString, setInt, or setLong to match the column.
Safety comes free. Values stay data, so they can't bend the query shape.
Speed comes too. The plan compiles once and the database reuses it.

beats.text: Say you fetch orders for one customer. You prepare the query with two placeholders, set the customer id and the status, then run it. Here's the non-obvious part. The shape is locked at prepare time, so even a weird id can't bend the query.

items: Counting from zero. JDBC parameters start at one, so the first setter is index one.
Building a fresh PreparedStatement inside a loop. You pay the compile cost every pass and lose the reuse.

speakable_v2.cap: So reach for PreparedStatement on any query with input. It's the safe choice and the fast one.
followup_handoff: How exactly does PreparedStatement stop SQL injection?
Why is a PreparedStatement faster when you run it many times?

questions.question: How do you use PreparedStatement for an INSERT query in JDBC?
questions.title: PreparedStatement for INSERT in JDBC
questions.direct_answer: Create a PreparedStatement with fixed INSERT SQL and ? placeholders, bind each value using one-based indexes, then call executeUpdate. The returned count normally reports affected rows, though driver/database behavior for special statements and success-without-count values should be respected. Use a transaction when the insert belongs to a larger atomic operation.

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether you can write a parameterized INSERT correctly.
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Off-by-one on 1-based parameter indexes, or using executeQuery for an INSERT.
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Note parameter indices are 1-based and executeUpdate returns the affected-row count.

sections.title: Executing an INSERT with PreparedStatement
sections.content:
try-with-resources closes the statement even when binding/execution fails. The connection's owner controls commit, rollback, and close/return-to-pool. A wrong setter can sometimes be converted by a driver rather than fail, which is another reason to match Java/JDBC types deliberately instead of relying on implicit conversion.

**Example.** INSERT INTO customer(name,email) VALUES (?,?) binds the name at index 1 and email at index 2, then executeUpdate reports the ordinary affected-row count.

sections.title: Quick revision
content: Placeholder 1 is the first parameter; JDBC indexes are one-based.
Bind values with suitable setters and handle SQL NULL explicitly.
Use executeUpdate for ordinary INSERT/UPDATE/DELETE statements.
Request generated keys explicitly when the created identifier is needed and supported.

sections.title: Interview answer
sections.content: For example, INSERT INTO customer(name,email) VALUES (?,?) is prepared once, then setString(1,name) and setString(2,email) bind data safely. executeUpdate() should report one affected row for a normal single-row insert. To read an identity value, prepare with Statement.RETURN_GENERATED_KEYS and inspect getGeneratedKeys after success.

sections.title: Parameterized INSERT at a Glance
sections.content:
blue|SQL|~placeholders|INSERT ... VALUES (?, ?)|one ? per value|order matters
emerald|Bind|~typed setters|setInt/setString|1-based index|match column type
amber|Execute|~executeUpdate|returns int row count|not executeQuery|for INSERT/UPDATE/DELETE
rose|Close|~try-with-resources|auto-close|no leaks|

sections.title: INSERT Recipe
sections.content:
| Step | Code |
|---|---|
| 1 | `prepareStatement("INSERT INTO users (name, age) VALUES (?, ?)")` |
| 2 | `ps.setString(1, name)` |
| 3 | `ps.setInt(2, age)` |
| 4 | `int rows = ps.executeUpdate()` |

sections.title: A parameterized INSERT
Common Mistakes
sections.content:
- **0-based indexing**: the first `?` is index **1**, not 0.
- **`executeQuery` for INSERT**: use `executeUpdate` (returns row count).
- **Wrong setter for the type**: `setString` for a number column can fail or mis-store.
- **Not closing**: wrap in try-with-resources.

executeUpdate tells the driver that no rows come back, just a count. It returns the number of rows you changed. For an INSERT that count's usually one.

items: Prepare the SQL with one question mark for each column you insert.
Bind the values with typed setters. The indexes start at one, not zero.
Call executeUpdate, not executeQuery, because an INSERT changes data.
Wrap it in try-with-resources so the statement closes on its own.

beats.text: Picture inserting one user row. You prepare the insert with three placeholders, set the name, email, and age, then call executeUpdate. Here's the non-obvious part. It returns one, the row count, so you'll know the write landed.

items: Calling executeQuery for an INSERT. The driver complains that no result set comes back.
Counting parameters from zero. The first placeholder is index one, so an off-by-one creeps in.

speakable_v2.cap: So prepare, bind one-based typed values, then call executeUpdate. That covers a clean parameterized INSERT.

questions.question: How do you set different data types in PreparedStatement?
questions.title: PreparedStatement Setter Methods for Different Data Types
questions.direct_answer: PreparedStatement setter methods bind Java values to one-based parameter positions. Use a setter that matches the intended SQL/JDBC type, such as setString, setInt, setLong, setBigDecimal, setDate, setTimestamp, setObject, or setNull. Binding keeps values separate from SQL syntax; it does not require every driver/database to literally compile the statement before values arrive.

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether you know the typed setters and how to bind NULL and dates correctly.
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Using setString for numbers/dates, or passing Java null instead of setNull.
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Use setBigDecimal for money and setTimestamp for datetimes; setNull for NULLs.

sections.title: Binding Java Values to PreparedStatement Parameters
sections.content:
PreparedStatement improves security because bound values are values, not identifier or operator text. Placeholders cannot stand for a table name, column name, ORDER BY direction, or an arbitrary SQL fragment; choose those from an allowlist and build only trusted fixed syntax. Plan/preparation behavior and performance depend on the driver, protocol, database, reuse, and server settings.

**Example.** Bind customer id with setLong, money with setBigDecimal, and a missing note with setNull using the intended VARCHAR SQL type.

sections.title: Quick revision
content: Parameter indexes start at 1, not 0.
Use BigDecimal for exact decimal values such as money.
Use setNull(index, Types.X) or a supported typed setObject call for SQL NULL.
Check JDBC 4.2 driver support when binding java.time values with setObject.

sections.title: Interview answer
sections.content: For example, INSERT INTO payment(customer_id, amount, paid_at, note) VALUES (?,?,?,?) can use setLong(1,id), setBigDecimal(2,amount), setObject(3,paidAt), and setNull(4,Types.VARCHAR). Passing null to a primitive setter is impossible, and blindly using setObject for every value can produce driver-specific type inference.

sections.title: Typed Setters at a Glance
sections.content:
blue|Numbers|~by precision|setInt/setLong|setDouble|setBigDecimal for money
emerald|Text/Bool|~basics|setString|setBoolean|
amber|Date/Time|~watch granularity|setDate = date only|setTimestamp = date+time|use java.sql types
rose|NULL|~explicit|setNull(idx, Types.X)|not bare null|specify the SQL type

sections.title: Setter Cheat Sheet
sections.content:
| Java/SQL type | Setter |
|---|---|
| int / Integer | `setInt` |
| money / decimal | `setBigDecimal` |
| String | `setString` |
| boolean | `setBoolean` |
| date+time | `setTimestamp` |
| NULL | `setNull(idx, Types.X)` |

sections.title: Binding several types (and NULL)
Common Mistakes
sections.content:
- **`setString` for numbers/dates**: causes type mismatches or string-stored values.
- **`double` for money**: use `setBigDecimal` to avoid rounding errors.
- **Bare Java `null`**: prefer `setNull(idx, Types.X)` so the driver knows the type.
- **`setDate` when you need time**: use `setTimestamp` to keep the time component.

seo.metaTitle: PreparedStatement Setter Methods for Different Data Types — java backend interview question | InterviewExplainer
seo.metaDescription: Interview answer for How do you set different data types in PreparedStatement? with a clear explanation, practical example, common mistakes, and follow-up questions.

speakable_v2.hook: Each SQL type has its own setter. The classics that bite are a double for money and a bare null.
speakable_v2.standard_example: A Java app binding typed values into an INSERT on a MySQL orders table

beats.text: PreparedStatement gives you one typed setter per SQL type. Each takes the parameter position and the value. The setter converts your Java value into the right SQL type.
Java types and SQL types don't line up cleanly. The typed setter handles that mapping for you. It's also good with the tricky bits, like decimals and timestamps.

items: Use setInt or setLong for whole numbers in INTEGER or BIGINT columns.
Use setBigDecimal for money. A double rounds badly and loses cents.
Use setString for text and setBoolean for true or false.
Use setDate for a date alone and setTimestamp for a date plus time.
Use setNull with the SQL type when the value is missing.

beats.text: Picture inserting an order row. You set the customer id as a long, the total as a BigDecimal, and the created time as a timestamp. Here's the non-obvious part. A missing note needs setNull with the type. That's a typed null, not a bare Java null.

items: Using setDate for a column that holds time too. It drops the time and stores midnight.
Passing a bare Java null. setNull with the SQL type is the portable, safe way.

speakable_v2.cap: So match the setter to the column. BigDecimal for money, timestamp for date-time, setNull for nullable.
followup_handoff: Why is setBigDecimal better than setDouble for money?
What is the difference between setDate and setTimestamp?

questions.question: How does PreparedStatement prevent SQL injection?
questions.title: How PreparedStatement Prevents SQL Injection
questions.direct_answer: PreparedStatement prevents a bound parameter value from changing the SQL grammar. The application prepares SQL with ? markers and supplies typed values through setXxx methods; the driver/database treats each binding as a value for that marker. The transport does not have to be two separate network messages, and the database does not have to compile once first for the security guarantee to hold.

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether you can explain the parse-then-bind mechanism, not just say 'it's safe'.
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Thinking PreparedStatement 'escapes' input rather than separating code from data.
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Clarify the query structure is fixed at prepare time, before any value is bound.

sections.title: Why Bound Parameters Stop Value Injection
sections.content:
PreparedStatement does not validate business meaning and does not protect SQL fragments constructed elsewhere. A query assembled as "ORDER BY " + requestParameter is unsafe even if its filter values are bound. Map a public sort key such as newest to a hard-coded SQL fragment instead.

Stored procedure calls and ORM queries need the same discipline: bind values through their parameter APIs. Parameterization prevents injection into query structure; least privilege limits damage if another defect remains.

sections.title: Quick revision
content: Placeholders represent values, not identifiers or SQL keywords.
Quotes and operators inside a bound string remain string data.
Concatenating any untrusted fragment before prepareStatement remains injectable.
Allow-list table names, column names, and sort directions that cannot be bound.

sections.title: Interview answer
sections.content:
With WHERE username = ? and a bound value alice' OR '1'='1, the condition still compares username to one literal value. The input cannot add an OR node to the statement's syntax. This remains true whether the driver uses a binary bind protocol or safely emulates preparation. The important contract is parameter binding, not a simplified wire-level story.

For example, SELECT * FROM users WHERE email = ? with ps.setString(1, input) treats x' OR '1'='1 as a string value, not as extra SQL syntax. Table names and sort directions still need allowlists because placeholders cannot represent identifiers.

sections.title: Why It's Safe
sections.content:
blue|Prepare|~structure fixed|parse + compile with ?|before values exist|query shape locked
emerald|Bind|~data only|setString/setInt|values into slots|never parsed as SQL
rose|Attack input|~harmless|' OR '1'='1|treated as a literal|can't add clauses
amber|Key idea|~code vs data|not escaping|separation|input never hits parser

sections.title: Concatenation: input IS the query
PreparedStatement: structure fixed before the value
Where This Applies
sections.content: Use parameter binding for **all** user-controlled input that reaches SQL. PreparedStatement handles **values** safely, but it does **not** parameterize identifiers like table/column names or `ORDER BY` directions — those must be validated against a whitelist, since they can't be bound as `?`.

seo.metaTitle: How PreparedStatement Prevents SQL Injection — java backend interview question | InterviewExplainer
seo.metaDescription: Interview answer for How does PreparedStatement prevent SQL injection? with a clear explanation, practical example, common mistakes, and follow-up questions.

speakable_v2.hook: PreparedStatement doesn't escape your input. It locks the query shape before the value arrives, so a sneaky string has nowhere to go.
speakable_v2.standard_example: A Java app searching a MySQL orders table by a user-supplied name with JDBC

beats.text: PreparedStatement splits the work into two steps. First the database parses the SQL with placeholders and fixes its shape. Then your values flow in as plain data.
Injection only works when input can change the query shape. By fixing the shape before any value shows up, PreparedStatement shuts that door.

items: Step one parses the SQL with placeholders. The shape's fixed right here.
Step two sends your values as data into those fixed slots.
A nasty value like quote OR one equals one stays a plain string.
It's separation of code and data, not character escaping.

beats.text: Say you search orders by name. You bind a quote OR one equals one comment as the name. Here's the non-obvious part. The database treats that whole thing as a literal name, so it matches nobody. Concatenation would have run it as code.

items: Gluing user input into the SQL before you prepare it. The query was already unsafe.
Trying to bind a table or column name with a placeholder. Only values bind, so check identifiers against a whitelist.

speakable_v2.cap: So the shape is locked before any value lands. That's why PreparedStatement is injection-proof.

questions.question: How do you execute a batch of INSERT statements using PreparedStatement?
questions.title: Batch Inserts with PreparedStatement
questions.direct_answer: Reuse one PreparedStatement, bind each row, call addBatch(), and periodically call executeBatch(). A transaction can make a chosen batch atomic and avoid committing each row separately. The correct commit and chunk size depends on rollback needs, memory, locks, log growth, driver limits, and database capacity; one enormous batch and one commit are not always best.

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether you can write a correct batched-insert loop.
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Calling executeUpdate inside the loop instead of addBatch, or never committing.
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Flush every N rows and commit once; handle rollback on failure.

sections.title: Batching PreparedStatement Inserts
sections.content:
Batching reduces client/server conversations but does not promise one network packet or one database statement. Drivers may rewrite batches only when configured. Always close the statement, and when using a pooled connection restore autoCommit and other changed state as required by the pool/ownership contract.

**Example.** Ten thousand import rows can be executed in 500-row batches, with commit boundaries chosen from the import's atomicity and restart requirements.

sections.title: Quick revision
content: Disable auto-commit only when the code owns that transaction boundary.
Call addBatch after binding every row and executeBatch at a measured chunk size.
Commit on success and roll back on failure; restore connection state before returning it to a pool.
Inspect BatchUpdateException update counts because drivers differ on partial success and generated keys.

sections.title: Interview answer
sections.content: For example, insert 10,000 audit rows in chunks of 500: bind two values, addBatch, execute/clear each 500, then commit the transaction if all chunks belong to one atomic unit. For a restartable import, committing each validated chunk may be a better requirement than rolling back all 10,000 rows.

sections.title: Batch INSERT at a Glance
sections.content:
blue|Prepare once|~outside loop|one PreparedStatement|reuse for all rows|
emerald|addBatch|~per row|bind then addBatch|queues the row|no round-trip
amber|executeBatch|~send together|one round-trip|flush every N|returns int[]
rose|Transaction|~atomic + fast|auto-commit off|commit once|rollback on error

sections.title: Batch INSERT Recipe
sections.content:
| Step | Code |
|---|---|
| 1 | `con.setAutoCommit(false)` |
| 2 | `prepareStatement("INSERT ... VALUES (?, ?)")` once |
| 3 | loop: `setXxx(...)`, `addBatch()`, flush every N |
| 4 | `executeBatch()`, then `con.commit()` |

sections.title: executeUpdate in the loop: one round-trip per row
addBatch + executeBatch: one round-trip per flush
Batched INSERT loop
Common Mistakes
sections.content:
- **`executeUpdate` in the loop**: defeats batching — use `addBatch`.
- **Re-preparing per row**: prepare once outside the loop.
- **No commit / auto-commit on**: each item commits separately.
- **One enormous batch**: flush every N rows to bound memory.

followup_questions: Why flush a batch every N rows?
What happens if you call executeUpdate inside the loop?
How does a transaction affect batch performance?

seo.metaTitle: Batch Inserts with PreparedStatement — java backend interview question | InterviewExplainer
seo.metaDescription: Interview answer for How do you execute a batch of INSERT statements using PreparedStatement? with a clear explanation, practical example, common mistakes, and follow-up questions.

speakable_v2.hook: A correct batch insert prepares once, queues rows with addBatch, fires them with executeBatch, and commits a single time.
speakable_v2.standard_example: A Java app bulk-inserting orders into a MySQL table with JDBC batching

beats.text: A batch groups many inserts into one trip to the database. You prepare the insert once, queue each row with addBatch, then send them together with executeBatch.
Each single executeUpdate is a full round trip. For thousands of rows that latency piles up. One batch and one commit cut the trips way down.

items: Turn off auto-commit first, so you own the transaction boundary.
Bind each row and call addBatch to queue it. Nothing runs yet.
Call executeBatch every thousand rows or so to flush and free memory.
Commit once at the end. Roll back in the catch block if anything fails.

beats.text: Picture importing fifty thousand orders from a file. You loop over the rows and addBatch each one. You flush every thousand rows. Here's the non-obvious part. Round trips drop from fifty thousand to about fifty. Spring's JdbcTemplate batchUpdate wraps this for you.

items: Leaving auto-commit on. Each row commits by itself and you lose the batch win.
Never clearing the batch after a flush. The queue grows until memory runs out.

speakable_v2.cap: So turn auto-commit off, addBatch in a loop, then commit once at the end.
followup_handoff: Why disable auto-commit before running a batch?
How does JdbcTemplate batchUpdate compare to raw batching?

questions.question: How do you retrieve auto-generated keys after an INSERT with PreparedStatement?
questions.title: Retrieving Auto-Generated Keys
questions.direct_answer: Request generated keys when creating the PreparedStatement, execute the insert, then read the ResultSet from getGeneratedKeys. The capability and returned columns are driver/database dependent; check DatabaseMetaData.supportsGetGeneratedKeys and vendor documentation. Some databases work better with SQL such as INSERT ... RETURNING or with explicit key column names.

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether you know the RETURN_GENERATED_KEYS + getGeneratedKeys flow.
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Re-querying with a SELECT to find the new id instead of using getGeneratedKeys.
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Note you must opt in at prepare time and the key comes back as a ResultSet.

sections.title: Retrieving Generated Keys with Driver Support
sections.content:
Some databases provide RETURNING and can return several generated columns directly. JDBC also allows supplying column indexes or names when preparing the statement. Batch insert key behavior varies more widely.

Never use SELECT MAX(id) to discover the inserted row; concurrent transactions make it incorrect. A connection-scoped vendor last-id function can be safer but remains vendor-specific. Prefer the driver's supported generated-key or RETURNING mechanism.

**Example.** prepareStatement(sql, Statement.RETURN_GENERATED_KEYS), executeUpdate(), then getGeneratedKeys() can return the created id when the driver supports it. Check next() before getLong(1), and use the database's RETURNING syntax when that is the clearer supported option.

sections.title: Quick revision
content: Pass Statement.RETURN_GENERATED_KEYS or requested key-column names at prepare time.
Call getGeneratedKeys after a successful execution and advance with next().
Support and result shape are not identical across drivers.
Keep insert and key retrieval on the same statement/connection; do not query a global last id unsafely.

sections.title: Interview answer
sections.content:
Connection.prepareStatement(sql, Statement.RETURN_GENERATED_KEYS) asks the driver to make keys available. After executeUpdate, try (ResultSet keys = ps.getGeneratedKeys()) { if (keys.next()) id = keys.getLong(1); }. That common pattern works with many identity columns, but it is not an unconditional JDBC promise that every generated value or batch key is returned. Verify driver support and column ordering.

For example, after INSERT INTO customer(name) VALUES (?) I request RETURN_GENERATED_KEYS, execute the statement, call keys.next(), and read keys.getLong(1). Driver support and multi-row key behavior must be verified.

sections.title: Generated Keys at a Glance
sections.content:
blue|Opt in|~at prepare time|RETURN_GENERATED_KEYS|second arg|required
emerald|Execute|~normal INSERT|executeUpdate()|inserts the row|
amber|getGeneratedKeys|~returns ResultSet|the new key(s)|rs.getLong(1)|1-based column
rose|Don't|~no SELECT MAX|racy under concurrency|use generated keys|reliable

sections.title: Generated Keys Recipe
sections.content:
| Step | Code |
|---|---|
| 1 | `prepareStatement(sql, Statement.RETURN_GENERATED_KEYS)` |
| 2 | `ps.setXxx(...)`, `ps.executeUpdate()` |
| 3 | `ResultSet keys = ps.getGeneratedKeys()` |
| 4 | `if (keys.next()) long id = keys.getLong(1)` |

sections.title: Getting the new auto-increment id
Common Mistakes
sections.content:
- **Forgetting `RETURN_GENERATED_KEYS`**: `getGeneratedKeys()` returns nothing without it.
- **`SELECT MAX(id)` after insert**: racy under concurrency — may return another session's id.
- **Not calling `keys.next()`**: the keys come back as a ResultSet you must advance.
- **Assuming column name**: read by index `getLong(1)` (key column naming varies).

followup_questions: Why is SELECT MAX(id) unreliable for getting the new id?
Do you need RETURN_GENERATED_KEYS at prepare time?
How do you read the generated key from the ResultSet?

seo.metaTitle: Retrieving Auto-Generated Keys — java backend interview question | InterviewExplainer
seo.metaDescription: Interview answer for How do you retrieve auto-generated keys after an INSERT with PreparedStatement? with a clear explanation, practical example, common mistakes, and follow-up questions.

speakable_v2.hook: Don't run SELECT MAX of id after an insert. Ask for the generated keys and read them back instead.
speakable_v2.standard_example: A Java app inserting an order and reading its new id with JDBC

beats.text: Retrieving a generated key means asking the database for the id it just assigned. You opt in at prepare time, run the insert, then read the key with getGeneratedKeys.
After you insert a parent row, you often need its id for child rows. The database assigns it during the insert, so reading it from the same statement is safe.

items: Pass RETURN_GENERATED_KEYS when you prepare the statement. This flags it to capture the id.
Run executeUpdate as usual to perform the insert.
Call getGeneratedKeys to get a small result set holding the new id.
Advance it with next, then read the id with getLong of column one.

beats.text: Picture inserting an order, then its line items. You insert the order with generated keys on, run it, and read order id forty-two. Here's the non-obvious part. SELECT MAX of id would race a concurrent insert and hand you the wrong id.

items: Using SELECT MAX of id after the insert. Another insert can sneak a higher id in between.
